transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-08-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CISO, KSL), Priya Rao (SRE Manager), Diego Morales (Infra), Hannah Lee (Legal)

Summary: quick readout on how Redwood behaves in a multi-region outage, KMS residency and key rotation questions, plus a request to exercise the runbook.

[00:00:05] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're going to run through the incident and resilience questions you sent over, and Samir will jump in on the KMS / logs side.
[00:00:15] Liam O'Connor: Thanks, Maya. We have a fairly tight compliance window — SOC 2 Type II and ISO scatter has to be reconciled with the third party inventory. Also we need to know how key custody works when using Redwood Private vs Hosted.
[00:00:30] Samir Patel: Sure. Quick note — Redwood's private deployment lets you bring your KMS (we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM via PKCS11 integrations), keys never leave customer control in the private mode. In hosted, keys are in Redwood KMS by default but we offer a customer-managed KMS option with envelope encryption and HSM-backed rotation.
[00:00:48] Priya Rao: So in hosted with customer-managed KMS, are we storing plaintext anywhere on Redwood systems? We need the assurance — RTO/RPO and data residency rules hinge on that.
[00:00:58] Samir Patel: No plaintext at rest for persisted artifacts. The token stream is transient on our inference nodes; we use prefix K V caching encrypted in-transit and at-rest. That said, logs may include redacted metadata unless you configure full audit logging to ship to your SIEM — we can show log redaction config.
[00:01:15] Diego Morales: When you say prefix K V cache, is that the same as KV cache? I've seen both on docs and wanted to confirm TTL and what survives a node failure.
[00:01:22] Samir Patel: Yeah, KV cache — apologies for the inconsistency. In practice KV cache is in the node memory and checkpointed to a shared datastore for dedicated/private. For hosted ephemeral nodes the cache may be lost on a node crash but the orchestration layer re-primes it from persistent partial checkpoints; RTO is impacted but replayable.
[00:01:40] Liam O'Connor: Let's talk RTO/RPO numbers. Our target for critical customer-facing routes is RTO < 5m and RPO near 0 for session context. Is that realistic with Redwood?
[00:01:51] Maya Chen: For dedicated pools with warmed KV checkpoints and prefix caching tuned, we've seen median recovery times under 3 minutes for single-node restarts. In hosted at base tier you should plan for longer; that's where routing to a warmed dedicated fallback or model variant helps.
[00:02:10] Priya Rao: Can you explain routing fallback? If a model endpoint goes down in eu-west, do you route to another region or a smaller quantized model in same region? What about data residency constraints — we can't cross-region for PHI.
[00:02:22] Samir Patel: Great question. Our routing policy engine supports several policies: region-first, cost-first, and residency-locked. For customers with EU-only residency we can lock routing to eu regions only. The failover options within region include spinning up a dedicated pool of compatible model variants or failing over to a pinned model variant in the same region. Cross-region is opt-in and we don't initiate cross-region failover for residency-constrained workloads.
[00:02:44] Hannah Lee: So legal needs this in writing — how fallback is blocked and the audit trail that proves we never left eu-west.
[00:02:52] Maya Chen: We'll include the routing policy spec and the audit log entries that indicate routing decisions. We'll also provide a sample SIEM export showing the region tag and model variant id for each request.
[00:03:05] Diego Morales: About audit logs: do you capture request / response hashes or payloads? For PCI / SOC we prefer only hashes with reference IDs.
[00:03:15] Samir Patel: By default, audit logs contain metadata and request ids; body content is redacted unless you enable full payload logging. For PCI customers we recommend payload offloading to a customer SIEM via forwarders and only keeping hashes in Redwood logs.
[00:03:30] Liam O'Connor: Let's move into incident response — escalation tiers and SLA impacts. What happens if the inference tier is degraded and latency breaches SLA?
[00:03:39] Maya Chen: Our public SLA for Dedicated is 99.95% uptime with credits and an escalation path. Operationally we have tiered alerts: P1 (service down / inability to serve tokens) triggers immediate page to our oncall infra team; P2 (severe degradation) has 15min response and P3 is next-business-day. We can share the escalation matrix.
[00:03:58] Priya Rao: Do you have a runbook that maps Redwood escalations to our pager and Slack channels? We need single-source-of-truth for the tabletop drill.
[00:04:08] Samir Patel: Yes. We can provision a shared runbook in the console which includes playbook steps, links to telemetry dashboards, and an incident command contact list. For private deployments you can configure webhooks to your incident manager (PagerDuty, OpsGenie).
[00:04:22] Diego Morales: During an outage, are there automatic fallbacks to a cheaper model to maintain availability? Would that require re-training or is it a model switch?
[00:04:31] Maya Chen: It's a model switch. You can pin a fallback variant that trades off some quality for lower resource consumption. The switch is atomic at the routing layer. We recommend smoke tests and canary routing to validate quality before full failover.
[00:04:45] Liam O'Connor: For the tabletop, we'd like to simulate KMS rotation failure mid-incident. What will that look like and what's the expected behavior of hosted vs private?
[00:04:55] Samir Patel: If KMS rotation or HSM becomes unavailable, for customer-managed KMS we rely on your key availability. In private deployments, keys are in your environment so Redwood can't rotate without your KMS API responses. If rotation API failures occur, requests will continue until key TTLs expire — there is a safe window. In hosted with Redwood-managed KMS, we have staged rotation with rollback window and dual-signed keys for fast rollback. We'll show the rotation timeline detail in the KMS doc.
[00:05:16] Priya Rao: Can you quantify the safe window and what happens to RTO if the KMS path is degraded?
[00:05:23] Samir Patel: Typical TTLs are configurable; we recommend 24h for rotation window in production. If the KMS path is unavailable past TTL, new sessions that require key unwrap will fail; older sessions can continue to use cached material for a short time. RTO for recovery after KMS restore depends on how many nodes need rekeying; for dedicated pools with concurrency under 100 nodes we've seen full recovery under 7-10 minutes if keys are re-imported.
[00:05:43] Hannah Lee: We need to align this with compliance docs — does Redwood support HSM attestation logs and key origin info for audits?
[00:05:51] Samir Patel: Yes, for HSM-backed keys we provide attestation statements and key origin entries. We'll include sample attestations and the type of metadata we store in audit logs.
[00:06:05] Maya Chen: Quick Q to KSL — what's your required RTO/RPO matrix? You mentioned <5m RTO for critical, do you have tier 2 values?
[00:06:14] Priya Rao: Tier 1 critical: RTO < 5 min, RPO 0 (session-level). Tier 2: RTO < 30 min, RPO < 5 min. We also want a list of 8 routes that are critical.
[00:06:26] Maya Chen: Great, action item — send that list and we'll map to dedicated pool sizing and warm checkpoint strategy.
[00:06:34] Diego Morales: On SLAs, does Redwood do per-route SLOs in the console? We want to see token-level latencies.
[00:06:41] Samir Patel: Yes, per-route SLOs and token-level percentiles are in the console. You can configure alerts on p50/p95/p99. The billing and cost pages also show cost per 1k tokens by model variant.
[00:06:54] Liam O'Connor: About RBAC and SSO — we plan to onboard via SAML SSO and want fine-grained RBAC for environment-level controls. Can you lock access for callouts that would export unredacted logs?
[00:07:05] Samir Patel: We support SCIM provisioning, SAML 2.0, and granular RBAC. We can create roles that can only view redacted audit logs; exports of full payloads can be restricted to certain roles. We also have session MFA enforcement hooks if you need step-up authentication for sensitive ops.
[00:07:22] Priya Rao: Any integration with our EDR / SIEM for incident enrichment?
[00:07:27] Samir Patel: We provide Logpush connectors and event webhooks, and we can ship structured JSON events to your SIEM. We also support correlation IDs so you can join Redwood traces with your tracing system.
[00:07:40] Diego Morales: A quick note — what's the expected behavior on a cloud provider-wide outage? Say GCP region has a control plane hit, do we automatically route to another cloud?
[00:07:48] Maya Chen: By default no, cross-cloud failover is not automatic. You must opt into a multi-region/multi-cloud routing policy. For customers that require multi-cloud resilience we provision dedicated capacity in two clouds and set up a primary/secondary routing with heartbeat health checks. That is typically part of an enterprise contract.
[00:08:05] Liam O'Connor: What's the SLA credit cadence and how do we dispute metrics? We need raw telemetry for disputes.
[00:08:12] Maya Chen: We provide raw telemetry exports for agreed reporting windows under enterprise agreements. SLA credits are processed per contract; dispute process includes sending our incident timeline, metrics, and customer-provided telemetry.
[00:08:24] Hannah Lee: We'll want to loop in procurement to negotiate the multi-cloud add-on if needed.
[00:08:30] Maya Chen: Noted.
[00:08:33] Samir Patel: On the topic of runbooks: we'll propose a 60-min tabletop that includes KMS rotation failure, model fallback, and a simulated node crash where KV checkpoints must be replayed. We'll act as SRE for Redwood and you play incident commander.
[00:08:48] Priya Rao: Sounds good. Can you also show the SIEM export and an example of redaction patterns? We need to approve the redaction regex before enabling full logs.
[00:08:57] Samir Patel: Yes we'll include sample lines and the redaction config.
[00:09:05] Diego Morales: Minor point — what's the maintenance window notification SLA? We don't want automatic upgrades during our high-traffic windows.
[00:09:12] Maya Chen: We schedule maintenance with at least 72-hour notice for non-critical updates. For critical security fixes we may have shorter windows but we coordinate the timing and can apply in staged canaries. For Dedicated customers you can pick a maintenance window.
[00:09:25] Liam O'Connor: OK, let's recap next steps.
[00:09:28] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to send SOC 2 Type II and ISO artifact summary; Samir to send KMS/HSM diagrams and sample audit logs; KSL to provide RTO/RPO matrix and critical routes; schedule tabletop week of Aug 23. Any additions?
[00:09:45] Hannah Lee: Legal wants the routing-policy lock statement in writing.
[00:09:50] Maya Chen: We'll add that to the deliverables.
[00:09:53] Liam O'Connor: One last question — can Redwood sign a short-term data processing addendum for the tabletop? We need it before the drill.
[00:10:00] Maya Chen: Yes, we have a standard DPA addendum we can send; we can flag it with legal for an expedited review.
[00:10:09] Priya Rao: Great, thanks all.
[00:10:11] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[00:10:30] (audio continues with scheduling and side-channel chats, then wrap)

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels and filler removed for clarity; some words transcribed phonetically, e.g., "K V" for KV cache, "runbok" present in raw notes.
